Funktionale Einordnung: AUTOSAR Classic Platform, Kommunikations- und Sicherheitsstack ( AUTOSAR_SWS_SecureOnboardCommunication , R4.3.1). Technischer Zweck: Spezifikation des Zusammenspiels zwischen Transportprotokoll ( CanTp ), PDU-Router ( PduR ), Sicherheitsmodul ( SecOC ) und Applikations-Kommunikationsschicht ( Com ) beim Empfang einer segmentierten, kryptografisch gesicherten I-PDU ( Secured I-PDU ). Es visualisiert die Entkopplung von TP-Rezeption (Einkopieren via TP-Puffer-APIs) und asynchroner Verifikation (MAC/Signaturprüfung im Task-Kontext) vor der Freigabe der authentischen I-PDU ( Authentic I-PDU ) an Com . 2. Komponenten, Entitäten & Schnittstellen Beteiligte Module («module»): CanTp : CAN Transport Protocol (Lower Layer, zuständig für Segmentierung, Flow Control und Reassemblierung). PduR : PDU Router (Routing-Instanz; vermittelt sowohl die TP-Rezeption als auch die anschließende IF-Rezeption). SecOC : Secure Onboard Communication (Verifikationsinstanz; Zwischenschicht für Authentizitäts- und Integritätsprüfung sowie Freshness-Management). Com : AUTOSAR Communication (Upper Layer; Signalextraktion und Bereitstellung an die RTE/Applikation). Schnittstellen & Interaktionen (APIs): TP-Empfangsschnittstelle (CanTp $\rightarrow$ PduR $\rightarrow$ SecOC): PduR_CanTpStartOfReception(...) $\rightarrow$ SecOC_

caption: Figure 27: Construction Order of Freshness Value for Verification 1

lines: 1. Diagrammtyp & Architektur-Kontext Diagrammtyp: Ablaufdiagramm / Aktivitätsdiagramm (Decision-Tree / Flowchart). Funktionale Einordnung: AUTOSAR Classic Platform, Communication Services Layer, Modul SecOC ( Secure Onboard Communication , SWS_SecOC). Technischer Zweck: Spezifikation der normativen Such- und Rekonstruktionsheuristik zur sender-empfängerseitigen Synchronisation von Freshness Values (FV) bei der PDU-Verifikation. Das Diagramm definiert die Stufe 1 eines mehrstufigen Heuristik-Algorithmus (Recovery-Window-Verfahren) zur Auflösung von Desynchronisationen des Reset Flags zwischen lokal persistiertem Zustand ( Latest value ) und übermitteltem Teilwert ( Received value ) innerhalb eines definierten Toleranzfensters von $X \in \{0, -1, +1, -2, +2\}$. 2. Komponenten, Entitäten & Schnittstellen Beteiligte Komponenten: SecOC-Modul ( SecOC ): Empfangsseitige PDU-Verifikation ( SecOC_RxIndication ) und Rekonstruktion des vollständigen Verification Freshness Value. Freshness Value Manager (FVM / SW-C): Stellt über die FVM-Schnittstelle ( SecOC_GetRxFreshnessValue ) den lokalen Zählerzustand bereit. Crypto Service Manager ( CSM ): Nachgelagerte MAC-/Signaturverifikation ( Csm_MacVerify ). Verarbeitete Datenstrukturen: Received value : Der in der gesicherten I-PDU (Secured I-PDU) unverschlüsselt übertragene, abgeschnittene Frische-Teilwert ( Truncated Freshness Value , hier: Reset Flag ). Latest value : Der im Empfänger-Knoten lokal gehaltene/synchronisierte Referenzzählerst

lines: 1. Diagrammtyp & Architektur-Kontext Statisches Architektur- und Schichtenmodell (AUTOSAR Layered View) des AUTOSAR Classic Krypto-Stacks mit vertikalen logischen Kanalstrukturen (Channels). Das Diagramm veranschaulicht die Einbettung des Crypto Service Managers (CSM) in die AUTOSAR-Basissoftware (BSW) sowie die hierarchische Weiterleitung kryptografischer Anfragen von der Applikationsebene bis zur zugrundeliegenden Hardware (Microcontroller/HSM) über standardisierte Zwischenschichten. 2. Komponenten, Entitäten & Schnittstellen Das Diagramm gliedert sich vertikal in Software- (SW) und Hardware-Ebenen (HW): - Application Layer : Beinhaltet mehrere Software-Komponenten/Applikationen ( App1 , App2 , App3 ), die spezifische Krypto-Dienste anfordern ( App1 : AES, App2 : AES, App3 : RSA). - Runtime Environment (RTE) : Vermittelt Schnittstellenaufrufe zwischen Application Layer und BSW. - Service Layer : Beherbergt den CSM (Standard) , der funktionale Krypto-Jobs entgegennimmt und über logische Kanäle verwaltet. - ECU Abstraction Layer : Enthält das Crypto Interface (CryIf), welches als Abstraktions- und Routing-Instanz dient. - Microcontroller Abstraction Layer (MCAL) : Enthält den hardwarenahen Crypto Driver (Crypto). - Complex Drivers (CDD) : Schichtenübergreifender Block parallel zu Service Layer, ECU Abstraction Layer und MCAL. - Microcontroller (HW) : Beinhaltet ein Hardware Security Module ( HSM ) mit Hardware-Krypto-Engines ( HW-AES , HW-RSA ). - Logische Kanäle & Schnittste

lines: 1. Diagrammtyp & Architektur-Kontext Klassifikation: UML-Sequenzdiagramm ( Sequence Diagram ). Architektur-Kontext: AUTOSAR Classic Platform (CP), Spezifikation AUTOSAR_SWS_SecureOnboardCommunication (SecOC, Release R4.3.1). Funktionaler Zweck: Modellierung des asynchron entkoppelten Sendeablaufs einer kryptografisch geschützten PDU ( Secured I-PDU ) im Modus der direkten Übertragung ( direct transmission ). Das Diagramm spezifiziert die Entkopplung zwischen synchronem Sendeaufruf aus dem oberen Kommunikationsstack und der zeitintensiven Generierung der Authentifizierungsdaten (Freshness Value + MAC) im zyklischen Task-Kontext ( SecOC_MainFunctionTx ). 2. Komponenten, Entitäten & Schnittstellen Beteiligte Module (Lebenslinien mit Stereotyp «module») Com (AUTOSAR COM): Sender der ungesicherten Nutzdaten ( Authentic I-PDU ); Empfänger der finalen Sendebestätigung ( Tx Confirmation ). PduR (PDU Router): Stateless Router zwischen Schichten; entkoppelt logisch über separate PDU-IDs die Strecken Com $\leftrightarrow$ SecOC und SecOC $\leftrightarrow$ CanIf . SecOC (Secure Onboard Communication): Kryptografisches Zwischenmodul. Puffert die Nutzdaten, erzeugt kryptografische Metadaten (Freshness / MAC) und setzt die Secured I-PDU zusammen. CanIf (CAN Interface): Bus-Schnittstelle zur Hardwareabstraktion; übernimmt die gesicherte PDU zur Weitergabe an den CAN-Treiber.

B. SecOC, TLS, DoIP oder SWCs via RTE). 2. lines: 1. Diagrammtyp & Architektur-Kontext PDU-Layout- und Datenstruktur-Diagramm aus der AUTOSAR Classic Platform (Modul Secure Onboard Communication, SecOC). Das Diagramm veranschaulicht die Bildung einer Secured I-PDU ohne Protokoll-Header durch Bit-Truncation (Abschneiden) von Frischewert und kryptografischem Authentifikator zur Bandbreitenoptimierung auf fahrzeuginternen Kommunikationsbussen (z. B. CAN, CAN FD, FlexRay). 2. Komponenten, Entitäten & Schnittstellen Das Diagramm definiert drei Basiskomponenten und deren Truncation-Parameter zur Bildung der resultierenden PDU: - Authentic I-PDU : Nutzdaten-PDU der oberen Kommunikationsschicht (unverändert übernommen). - Freshness Value (im Schaubild typografisch als „Feshness Value“ bezeichnet): Vollständiger Frischewert (z. caption: Figure 23: Format of the synchronization message (TripResetSyncMsg)

lines: 1. Diagrammtyp & Architektur-Kontext - Diagrammtyp: PDU-Payload-Layout / Bitfeld-Strukturdiagramm (Network Layer Frame Layout). - Technischer Zweck: Spezifikation der Serialisierungsstruktur der Synchronisationsnachricht ( TripResetSyncMsg ) innerhalb des AUTOSAR Secure Onboard Communication ( SecOC ) Moduls. - Funktionale Einordnung: Dient im zeit- und ereignisbasierten Freshness-Value-Management (FVM) zur netzwerkweiten Verteilung des aktuellen globalen Zählerzustands ( Trip Counter und Reset Counter ) von einem zentralen Synchronisations-Master an alle Synchronisations-Slaves. Dies stellt die zeitliche Monotonie sicher und verhindert Replay-Angriffe auf gesicherte PDUs ( Secured I-PDUs ). 2. Komponenten, Entitäten & Schnittstellen - Bit- & Byte-Orientierung: - MSB (Most Significant Bit/Byte, links) bis LSB (Least Significant Bit/Byte, rechts); Serialisierung erfolgt in Network Byte Order (Big-Endian). - Nutzdaten-Entitäten (Payload-Felder): - Trip Counter : Oberer Zählerwert (z. B. persistent gespeicherte Anzahl der Fahr- bzw. Zündungszyklen). - Länge: Konfigurierbar über den Parameter TripCntLength (in Bits). - Reset Counter : Mittlerer Zählerwert (z. B. Anzahl der Resets / Neustarts des Masters innerhalb desselben Trips). - Länge: Konfigurierbar über den Parameter ResetCntLength (in Bits). - Authenticator : Kryptografische Prüfsumme (Truncated MAC) zum Schutz der Authentizität und Integrität der Zählerwerte. - Länge: Konfigurierbar über den Parameter SecOCAuthInfoTxLengt

lines: 1. Diagrammtyp & Architektur-Kontext Diagrammtyp: Topologisches Architektur- und Rollendiagramm (Netzwerk-/Systemkonfigurationsmodell auf Steuergeräteebene). Technischer Zweck: Spezifikation der logischen Rollenverteilung und Synchronisationsbeziehungen für das zentralisierte Freshness Value Management (FVM) gemäß AUTOSAR SecOC ( Secure Onboard Communication , Anhang B / Single FV Management Master Method). Funktionale Einordnung: Sicherstellung des Schutzes gegen Replay-Angriffe bei gesicherter I-PDU-Übertragung. Das Diagramm definiert das Szenario, in welchem eine dedizierte Master-Instanz die systemweite Frischebasis (z. B. Master-Sync-Zähler, Trip/Reset-Counter) vorgibt, während Sender- und Empfänger-Steuergeräte bezüglich der Frischeverwaltung als abhängige Slaves agieren. 2. Komponenten, Entitäten & Schnittstellen FV management master ECU: Rolle: Zentrale Quelle der Frische (Freshness Master). Funktion: Generiert, inkrementiert und broadcastet Master-Synchronisationsnachrichten (Sync-PDUs) zur Re-Synchronisation der lokalen Freshness-Werte im Fahrzeugnetzwerk. Slave ECU (Gruppierung / logische Abstraktion): Umfasst alle Steuergeräte, die ihren Frischezustand nicht autonom als absolute Zeitbasis generieren, sondern sich auf den Master synchronisieren. Sender ECU (Teilmenge von Slave ECU): Rolle: Transmitter der Secured I-PDU. Schnittstellen / Bausteine: PduR , SecOC , Csm (Crypto Service Manager), lokaler FVM-Client. caption: Figure 7.1: AUTOSAR Layered View with CSM

lines: ### 1. Diagrammtyp & Zweck

- **Diagrammtyp:** Statisches Architektur- und Schichtenmodell (AUTOSAR Layered Software Architecture) mit einer Makro-Gesamtsicht (links) und einer detaillierten Zoom-In-Ansicht des Krypto-Subsystems (rechts).

- **Technischer Zweck:** Das Diagramm spezifiziert die Verortung und Einbettung des **Crypto Service Managers (CSM)** und des gesamten AUTOSAR-Krypto-Stacks innerhalb der Classic Platform (CP, z. B. R24-11). Es verdeutlicht die vertikale Schichtung vom Application Layer über die RTE, den BSW-Service-Layer (CSM), die Hardware-Abstraktion (Crypto Interface / CryIf, externe & SW-Treiber) bis zur MCAL-Treiberebene und den zugrundeliegenden Hardware-Sicherheitsmodulen (SHE, HSM, externe Krypto-ICs via SPI).
### 2. Beteiligte Komponenten & Entitäten
#### A. Makro-Schichtenansicht (Linke Seite – AUTOSAR BSW-Stack)
- **Application Layer:** Beherbergt die AUTOSAR Software Components (SWCs).
- **Runtime Environment (RTE):** Entkoppelt Applikation und Basissoftware (BSW).
- **Services Layer:**
- *System Services*
- *Memory Services*
- **Crypto Services** *(hervorgehoben; Beherbergung des CSM)*
- *Communication Services*
- **ECU Abstraction Layer:**
- *On-board Device Abstraction*
- *Memory Hardware Abstraction*
- **Crypto Hardware Abstraction** *(hervorgehoben; Beherbergung von CryIf und externen Treibern)*
- *Communication Hardware Abstraction*
- *I/O Hardware Abstraction*
- **Microcontroller Abstraction Layer (MCAL):**
- *Microcontroller Drivers*
- *Memory Drivers*
- **Crypto Drivers** *(hervorgehoben; hardwarenahe Krypto-Treiber)*
- *Communication Drivers*
- *I/O Drivers*
- **Complex Drivers (CDD):** Schichtenübergreifender Block zur direkten Hardwareanbindung mit Umgehung der Standard-Stacks.
- **Microcontroller ($\mu\text{C}$):** Physikalische Hardwareplattform.
#### B. Detailansicht des Krypto-Stacks (Rechte Seite)
- **Crypto Services (Service Layer):**
- `Crypto Service Manager` (CSM): Zentraler Management- und API-Baustein für kryptografische Dienste.
- **Crypto Hardware Abstraction Layer:**
- `Crypto Interface` (CryIf): Abstraktions- und Routing-Modul zwischen CSM und den konkreten Treibern.
- `External Crypto Driver`: Treiber für externe Hardware-Sicherheitsbausteine (z. B. Secure Element, TPM).
- `Crypto Driver (SW-based)`: Software-Krypto-Bibliothek/Treiber zur Ausführung von Algorithmen ohne Hardware-Beschleuniger.
- **Driver Layer (MCAL / BSW):**
- `Crypto Drivers`: Mehrere Instanzen hardwarenaher MCAL-Krypto-Treiber (zwei vertikale Blöcke `Crypto Driver`).
- `Communication Drivers`: Enthält den `SPIHandlerDriver` (SPI-Handler/Treiber des MCAL).
- **Microcontroller ($\mu\text{C}$) / Hardware Peripherals:**
- `SHE` (Secure Hardware Extension): On-Chip-Sicherheitsperipherie.
- `HSM` (Hardware Security Module): Leistungsfähiger On-Chip-Sicherheitscrozessor.
- `\mu C`: Hauptprozessorkern.
- `SPI`: Serielle Peripherieschnittstelle zur Anbindung externer Krypto-Hardware.
### 3. Technische Abläufe & Beziehungen
- **Auftragserteilung (Application $\rightarrow$ CSM):**

- Eine SWC initiiert kryptografische Operationen (z. B. Hashing, Signaturprüfung, MAC-Generierung, Ver-/Entschlüsselung, Key-Management) über AUTOSAR-Ports an die RTE, welche die Service-Funktionen des `Crypto Service Manager` (CSM) aufruft (z. B. `Csm_JobStart()`, `Csm_JobProcess()`).
- **Standardisiertes Dispatching (CSM $\rightarrow$ CryIf):**
- Der CSM leitet Krypto-Jobs schichtabwärts an das `Crypto Interface` (`CryIf`) weiter. Die Schnittstelle zwischen CSM und CryIf abstrahiert vollständig von der tatsächlichen Ausführungsumgebung.
- **Kanal- und Treiber-Routing (CryIf $\rightarrow$ Crypto Driver Implementierungen):**
- Das CryIf fungiert als Multiplexer und routet Anfragen anhand der Konfiguration (CryIfChannel / CryIfKey) an einen der drei Zielpfade:
1. **Interner Hardwarepfad:** Aufruf des zuständigen MCAL `Crypto Driver` (z. B. via `Crypto_ProcessJob()`), der direkt auf On-Chip-Hardwareerweiterungen (`SHE` oder `HSM`) zugreift.
2. **Reiner Softwarepfad:** Weiterleitung an den `Crypto Driver (SW-based)`, der Berechnungen auf dem Hauptprozessor durchführt.
3. **Externer Hardwarepfad:** Weiterleitung an den `External Crypto Driver` in der Hardware-Abstraktionsschicht.
- **Inter-Modul-Kommunikation für externe Krypto-Hardware:**
- Der `External Crypto Driver` greift über eine gerichtete Assoziation (dargestellt durch den Pfeil im Diagramm) auf den `SPIHandlerDriver` der *Communication Drivers* (MCAL) zu.
- Über den SPI-Bus kommuniziert dieser Treiber mit externen Krypto-Controllern oder Secure Elements außerhalb des Mikrocontrollers.
- **Rückmelde- und Callback-Ketten:**
- Bei asynchroner Abarbeitung melden die Treiber die Beendigung via Callbacks über CryIf zurück an den CSM, welcher die Fertigstellung über die RTE an die aufrufende SWC signalisiert.
### 4. Besondere technische Details & Normative Hinweise
- **Architektur-Evolution (AUTOSAR 4.3+ Redesign):**

- Das Diagramm zeigt das mit AUTOSAR 4.3 eingeführte, flexible Krypto-Architekturmodell mit `CryIf`. Frühere AUTOSAR-Releases besaßen eine starre 1:1-Bindung zwischen CSM und einem proprietären Krypto-Treiber.
- **Multi-Driver- und Heterogenitätsunterstützung:**
- Durch CryIf können beliebig viele unterschiedliche Krypto-Treiber (parallele MCAL-Treiber, SW-Treiber und externe Hardware-Treiber) nebeneinander betrieben werden.
- **Schichtenübergreifender Zugriff des External Crypto Drivers:**

- Der `External Crypto Driver` befindet sich in der *Crypto Hardware Abstraction* und nutzt normgerecht einen Treiber einer Nachbardomäne (*Communication Drivers / SPIHandlerDriver* im MCAL), um Hardware-Peripherie auf der Platine anzusprechen.
- **Entkopplung von Algorithmus und Keystore:**

- Das Konzept erlaubt die Trennung von Key-Speicherorten und Algorithmen: Schlüssel können geschützt im HSM/SHE oder externen SE verbleiben, während der CSM über abstrakte Key-IDs (`CryptoKeyId`) operiert, ohne sensitive Schlüsseldaten im RAM offenzulegen.
- **Synchrone vs. Asynchrone Job-Verarbeitung:**
- Der CSM unterstützt sowohl blockierende synchrone Abfragen als auch asynchrone Queuing-Mechanismen mit Priorisierung (Job-Priorities).
### 5. Zusammenfassung für Entwickler

Für Entwickler und Systemintegratoren zeigt das Diagramm, dass Applikationen über den CSM kryptografische Funktionen vollständig hardwareagnostisch nutzen können. Integratoren müssen lediglich im CryIf das Routing zwischen logischen Krypto-Jobs und den physischen Treibern (HSM, SHE, Software oder extern via SPI) konfigurieren, wodurch sich Sicherheitsmodule ohne Codeänderungen in der Applikationsschicht austauschen oder erweitern lassen.

Es verdeutlicht die vertikale Schichtung vom Application Layer über die RTE, den BSW-Service-Layer (CSM), die Hardware-Abstraktion (Crypto Interface / CryIf, externe & SW-Treiber) bis zur MCAL-Treiberebene und den zugrundeliegenden Hardware-Sicherheitsmodulen (SHE, HSM, externe Krypto-ICs via SPI).

---

### 2. Beteiligte Komponenten & Entitäten

#### A. Makro-Schichtenansicht (Linke Seite – AUTOSAR BSW-Stack)
- **Application Layer:** Beherbergt die AUTOSAR Software Components (SWCs).
- **Runtime Environment (RTE):** Entkoppelt Applikation und Basissoftware (BSW).
- **Services Layer:**
  - *System Services*
  - *Memory Services*
  - **Crypto Services** *(hervorgehoben; Beherbergung des CSM)*
  - *Communication Services*
- **ECU Abstraction Layer:**
  - *On-board Device Abstraction*
  - *Memory Hardware Abstraction*
  - **Crypto Hardware Abstraction** *(hervorgehoben; Beherbergung von CryIf und externen Treibern)*
  - *Communication Hardware Abstraction*
  - *I/O Hardware Abstraction*
- **Microcontroller Abstraction Layer (MCAL):**
  - *Microcontroller Drivers*
  - *Memory Drivers*
  - **Crypto Drivers** *(hervorgehoben; hardwarenahe Krypto-Treiber)*
  - *Communication Drivers*
  - *I/O Drivers*
- **Complex Drivers (CDD):** Schichtenübergreifender Block zur direkten Hardwareanbindung mit Umgehung der Standard-Stacks.
- **Microcontroller ($\mu\text{C}$):** Physikalische Hardwareplattform.

#### B. Detailansicht des Krypto-Stacks (Rechte Seite)
- **Crypto Services (Service Layer):**
  - `Crypto Service Manager` (CSM): Zentraler Management- und API-Baustein für kryptografische Dienste.
- **Crypto Hardware Abstraction Layer:**
  - `Crypto Interface` (CryIf): Abstraktions- und Routing-Modul zwischen CSM und den konkreten Treibern.
  - `External Crypto Driver`: Treiber für externe Hardware-Sicherheitsbausteine (z. B. Secure Element, TPM).
  - `Crypto Driver (SW-based)`: Software-Krypto-Bibliothek/Treiber zur Ausführung von Algorithmen ohne Hardware-Beschleuniger.
- **Driver Layer (MCAL / BSW):**
  - `Crypto Drivers`: Mehrere Instanzen hardwarenaher MCAL-Krypto-Treiber (zwei vertikale Blöcke `Crypto Driver`).
  - `Communication Drivers`: Enthält den `SPIHandlerDriver` (SPI-Handler/Treiber des MCAL).
- **Microcontroller ($\mu\text{C}$) / Hardware Peripherals:**
  - `SHE` (Secure Hardware Extension): On-Chip-Sicherheitsperipherie.
  - `HSM` (Hardware Security Module): Leistungsfähiger On-Chip-Sicherheitscrozessor.
  - `\mu C`: Hauptprozessorkern.
  - `SPI`: Serielle Peripherieschnittstelle zur Anbindung externer Krypto-Hardware.

---

### 3. Technische Abläufe & Beziehungen

- **Auftragserteilung (Application $\rightarrow$ CSM):**
  - Eine SWC initiiert kryptografische Operationen (z. B. Hashing, Signaturprüfung, MAC-Generierung, Ver-/Entschlüsselung, Key-Management) über AUTOSAR-Ports an die RTE, welche die Service-Funktionen des `Crypto Service Manager` (CSM) aufruft (z. B. `Csm_JobStart()`, `Csm_JobProcess()`).
- **Standardisiertes Dispatching (CSM $\rightarrow$ CryIf):**
  - Der CSM leitet Krypto-Jobs schichtabwärts an das `Crypto Interface` (`CryIf`) weiter. Die Schnittstelle zwischen CSM und CryIf abstrahiert vollständig von der tatsächlichen Ausführungsumgebung.
- **Kanal- und Treiber-Routing (CryIf $\rightarrow$ Crypto Driver Implementierungen):**
  - Das CryIf fungiert als Multiplexer und routet Anfragen anhand der Konfiguration (CryIfChannel / CryIfKey) an einen der drei Zielpfade:
    1. **Interner Hardwarepfad:** Aufruf des zuständigen MCAL `Crypto Driver` (z. B. via `Crypto_ProcessJob()`), der direkt auf On-Chip-Hardwareerweiterungen (`SHE` oder `HSM`) zugreift.
    2. **Reiner Softwarepfad:** Weiterleitung an den `Crypto Driver (SW-based)`, der Berechnungen auf dem Hauptprozessor durchführt.
    3. **Externer Hardwarepfad:** Weiterleitung an den `External Crypto Driver` in der Hardware-Abstraktionsschicht.
- **Inter-Modul-Kommunikation für externe Krypto-Hardware:**
  - Der `External Crypto Driver` greift über eine gerichtete Assoziation (dargestellt durch den Pfeil im Diagramm) auf den `SPIHandlerDriver` der *Communication Drivers* (MCAL) zu.
  - Über den SPI-Bus kommuniziert dieser Treiber mit externen Krypto-Controllern oder Secure Elements außerhalb des Mikrocontrollers.
- **Rückmelde- und Callback-Ketten:**
  - Bei asynchroner Abarbeitung melden die Treiber die Beendigung via Callbacks über CryIf zurück an den CSM, welcher die Fertigstellung über die RTE an die aufrufende SWC signalisiert.

---

### 4. Besondere technische Details & Normative Hinweise

- **Architektur-Evolution (AUTOSAR 4.3+ Redesign):**
  - Das Diagramm zeigt das mit AUTOSAR 4.3 eingeführte, flexible Krypto-Architekturmodell mit `CryIf`. Frühere AUTOSAR-Releases besaßen eine starre 1:1-Bindung zwischen CSM und einem proprietären Krypto-Treiber.
- **Multi-Driver- und Heterogenitätsunterstützung:**
  - Durch CryIf können beliebig viele unterschiedliche Krypto-Treiber (parallele MCAL-Treiber, SW-Treiber und externe Hardware-Treiber) nebeneinander betrieben werden.
- **Schichtenübergreifender Zugriff des External Crypto Drivers:**
  - Der `External Crypto Driver` befindet sich in der *Crypto Hardware Abstraction* und nutzt normgerecht einen Treiber einer Nachbardomäne (*Communication Drivers / SPIHandlerDriver* im MCAL), um Hardware-Peripherie auf der Platine anzusprechen.
- **Entkopplung von Algorithmus und Keystore:**
  - Das Konzept erlaubt die Trennung von Key-Speicherorten und Algorithmen: Schlüssel können geschützt im HSM/SHE oder externen SE verbleiben, während der CSM über abstrakte Key-IDs (`CryptoKeyId`) operiert, ohne sensitive Schlüsseldaten im RAM offenzulegen.
- **Synchrone vs. Asynchrone Job-Verarbeitung:**
  - Der CSM unterstützt sowohl blockierende synchrone Abfragen als auch asynchrone Queuing-Mechanismen mit Priorisierung (Job-Priorities).

---

### 5. Zusammenfassung für Entwickler

Für Entwickler und Systemintegratoren zeigt das Diagramm, dass Applikationen über den CSM kryptografische Funktionen vollständig hardwareagnostisch nutzen können. Integratoren müssen lediglich im CryIf das Routing zwischen logischen Krypto-Jobs und den physischen Treibern (HSM, SHE, Software oder extern via SPI) konfigurieren, wodurch sich Sicherheitsmodule ohne Codeänderungen in der Applikationsschicht austauschen oder erweitern lassen.

Diagrammtyp & Architektur-Kontext - Klassifikation: Hybrides Architektur- und Datenfluss-Schichtenmodell mit integrierter PDU-Struktur-Transformation (AUTOSAR Classic Platform BSW). - Technischer Zweck: Spezifikation der architektonischen Einbindung des BSW-Moduls SecOC (Secure Onboard Communication) neben dem PDU-Router ( PduR ) und Veranschaulichung der strukturellen Kapselung einer Authentic I-PDU in eine Secured I-PDU für TX- und RX-Pfade. - Funktionale Einordnung: Verortung in der Kommunikationsschicht (Services Layer / Communication Services). SecOC agiert als kryptografischer Mediator/Transformator, der transparent zwischen Quell- und Zielmodulen eingehängt wird, ohne dass obere Schichten (wie AUTOSAR COM) Details über Authentifizierungsmechanismen (MAC/Signatur, Frische-Werte) kennen müssen. 2. Komponenten, Entitäten & Schnittstellen - Akteure & BSW-Module: - Upper Layer SW Module : Repräsentiert I-PDU-Quellen bzw. -Senken der Applikationsebene (typisch: AUTOSAR COM , alternativ Dcm oder Gateway-Module). - PDUR (PDU Router): Zentraler Dispatcher und Entkoppler. Verwaltet Routing-Tabellen zwischen oberen Modulen, SecOC und unteren Kommunikationsmodulen. - SecOC (Secure Onboard Communication): Führt Authentifizierung, PDU-Konstruktion/-Dekonstruktion, Frische-Management (Freshness Value Counter/FVM-Kopplung) und CSM-/Crypto-Stack-Aufrufe aus. - Lower Layer Communication Modules : Transportschichten und Bus-Interfaces (z. B. CanIf , CanTp , LinIf , FrIf , SoAd ). - Da

Reference value : Der aktuell höchste, erfolgreich verifizierte Freshness Value (oberer Referenzpunkt). lines: 1. Diagrammtyp & Architektur-Kontext Diagrammtyp: UML-Sequenzdiagramm (Interaktionsdiagramm mit Modul-Lebenslinien und Ausführungsfokus/Execution Specifications). Technischer Zweck: Spezifikation des Zusammenspiels und der Kontrollfluss-Entkopplung bei getriggerter Übertragung ( Triggered Transmission , z. B. FlexRay via FrIf ) von gesicherten I-PDUs ( Secured I-PDUs ) unter Einbindung von Com , PduR und SecOC nach AUTOSAR Classic R4.3.1. Funktionale Einordnung: Entkopplung der asynchronen, oberen Sendeschicht ( Com , rein ereignis- oder zyklusbasiertes Transmit ) von der zeitsynchronen, schlitzbasierten Übertragung der unteren Schicht ( FrIf , TriggerTransmit ). SecOC agiert als zustandsbehaftetes Puffer- und Authentifizierungsglied ( Decoupling Buffer ), um kryptografische Berechnungen zeitgerecht vor dem Bus-Trigger bereitzustellen. 2. Komponenten, Entitäten & Schnittstellen Akteure & Module (Stereotyp «module» ) Com : AUTOSAR Communication Module; initiiert den Sendeauftrag für die Nutzdaten ( Authentic I-PDU ) und empfängt die finale Tx-Bestätigung. PduR : PDU Router; verteilt I-PDUs zwischen oberen Kommunikationsmodulen, SecOC und Bus-Interfaces. SecOC : Secure Onboard Communication; puffert Rohdaten, führt die kryptografische Authentifizierung (MAC-Erzeugung, Freshness Value) aus und bedient die getriggerte Abfrage. FrIf : FlexRay Interface; untere Kommunikationsschicht, steuert den physischen Buszugriff im FlexRay-Kommunikationszyklus.

lines: 1. Diagrammtyp & Architektur-Kontext Klassifikation: Schichtenmodell / Statischer API-Aufrufbaum (Call Tree) mit funktionaler Pfadtrennung (Job-based vs. Direct API). Technischer Zweck: Darstellung der Schnittstellenarchitektur des AUTOSAR Crypto Stacks (Classic Platform) über drei Abstraktionsebenen: 1. CSM ( Crypto Service Manager , Service Layer, BSW) 2. CryIf ( Crypto Interface , Abstraktionsschicht zur Treiber-Entkopplung) 3. Crypto ( Crypto Driver , MCAL / hardware- oder softwarebasierte Ausführungsschicht) Funktionale Einordnung: Entkopplung kryptografischer Operationen (Berechnungen, Verschlüsselung, Signaturen) von administrativen Schlüsselverwaltungsoperationen (Key Management). --- 2. Komponenten, Entitäten & Schnittstellen Schichten (vertikal von oben nach unten) CSM (Blau/Violett): BSW-Dienstkomponente; stellt die applikationsnahe Schnittstelle (C-API und RTE-Service-Ports) bereit. CryIf (Grün): Vermittlungs- und Abstraktionsschicht; routet Anfragen anhand logischer Channel- und Key-IDs an den zuständigen Treiber. Crypto Driver (Rot/Koralle): MCAL-/Treiberebene; greift auf Hardwarebeschleuniger (HSM, SHE, Secure Core) oder Software-Krypto-Bibliotheken zu.

Crypto Driver (Rot/Koralle): MCAL-/Treiberebene; greift auf Hardwarebeschleuniger (HSM, SHE, Secure Core) oder Software-Krypto-Bibliotheken zu.

Komponenten, Entitäten & Schnittstellen - Module / Lifelines («module»): - Com : Oberer Kommunikations-Layer; initiiert die Übertragung großer Nutzdaten-I-PDUs und stellt Daten segmentweise via TP-Copy-Interface bereit. - PduR : PDU-Router; entkoppelt Schichten und routet TP- und IF-APIs anhand der Routing-Tabellen zwischen Quell- und Zielmodulen. - SecOC : Secure Onboard Communication; verwaltet Zwischenpufferung, Freshness-Werte, MAC-/Signaturgenerierung (Authentifizierung) und bedient sowohl obere als auch untere TP-Schnittstellen. - CanTp : CAN Transport Protocol; segmentiert die von SecOC übergebene Secured I-PDU für den physikalischen CAN-Bus (Tx-Pufferabruf). - Schnittstellen & Service-APIs: - Tx-Initiierung (Upper Layer): - PduR_ComTransmit(Std_ReturnType, PduIdType, const PduInfoType ) - SecOC_TpTransmit() - Payload-Abruf durch

Application Layer & Runtime Environment (RTE): - Software-Komponenten (SWCs) greifen über standardisierte AUTOSAR-Ports (Client-Server-Interfaces) und die RTE auf kryptografische Dienste zu. 2. Crypto Services Layer: - Crypto Service Manager (CSM): Zentraler, hersteller- und hardwareunabhängiger Service-Endpunkt. Stellt standardisierte C- und AUTOSAR-APIs für kryptografische Primitiven bereit (Hash, MAC, Ver-/Entschlüsselung, Signatur, Key Management, Zufallszahlen). 3. Crypto Hardware Abstraction Layer: - Crypto Interface (CRYIF): Abstraktions- und Dispatching-Instanz. Leitet Jobs aus dem CSM anhand statisch konfigurierter Channel-Mappings an den zuständigen Treiber weiter. -

Diagrammtyp & Architektur-Kontext - Klassifikation: AUTOSAR-Schichtenmodell / Statisches Architektur-Blockdiagramm (Layered Software Architecture View) mit selektiver Breakout-Detaillierung des Krypto-Subsystems (AUTOSAR Classic Platform ab Release 4.3 / 4.4). - Technischer Zweck & Gesamtsystem-Einordnung: Visualisierung der vertikalen Integration des modularen AUTOSAR-Krypto-Stacks über alle BSW-Schichten hinweg – vom Application Layer über Services Layer, ECU Abstraction Layer und Microcontroller Abstraction Layer (MCAL) bis hin zur Hardware-Ebene (Host-µC, integrierte On-Chip-Sicherheitsmodule und externe Peripherie). 2. Komponenten, Entitäten & Schnittstellen Das Diagramm gliedert sich in eine Übersicht der Gesamtschichten (links) und die funktionale Modulzerlegung des Crypto-Stacks (rechts): 1. Application Layer & Runtime Environment (RTE): - Software-Komponenten (SWCs) greifen über standardisierte AUTOSAR-Ports (Client-Server-Interfaces) und die RTE auf kryptografische Dienste zu. 2. Crypto Services Layer: - Crypto Service Manager (CSM): Zentraler, hersteller- und hardwareunabhängiger Service-Endpunkt. Stellt standardisierte C- und AUTOSAR-APIs für kryptografische Primitiven bereit (Hash, MAC, Ver-/Entschlüsselung, Signatur, Key Management, Zufallszahlen). 3. Crypto Hardware Abstraction Layer: - Crypto Interface (CRYIF): Abstraktions- und Dispatching-Instanz. Leitet Jobs aus dem CSM anhand statisch konfigurierter Channel-Mappings an den zuständigen Treiber weiter. -

lines: 1. Diagrammtyp & Architektur-Kontext Klassifikation: Daten- und Kontrollflussdiagramm (funktionales Wirkungs- und PDU-Konstruktionsmodell) auf BSW-/RTE-/Applikationsebene. Technischer Zweck: Schematische Darstellung des symmetrischen kryptografischen Authentifizierungs- und Verifikationsprozesses in AUTOSAR SecOC ( Secure Onboard Communication , SWS-ID-Bereich SWS_SecOC_ ) zwischen Sender- und Empfänger-ECU zur Absicherung von I-PDUs gegen Replay-, Injection- und Masquerading-Angriffe. Architektur-Einordnung: Einbettung des BSW-Moduls SecOC zwischen PduR (PDU Router) und Cryptographic Service Manager (CSM) / Crypto Stack, mit Schnittstelle über die RTE zum Freshness Value Manager (FVM) in der Application Layer. 2. Komponenten, Entitäten & Schnittstellen Akteure & Module: Application Layer / FVM ( Freshness Value Manager ): Software-Component (SW-C), zuständig für Generierung, Synchronisation und Bereitstellung monoton steigender Frischewerte (Zähler, Timestamps oder Trip-Counters). RTE ( Runtime Environment ): Vermittelt standardisierte AUTOSAR-Client/Server- bzw. Sender/Receiver-Interfaces zwischen FVM (Applikationsebene) und SecOC-BSW. SecOC BSW-Modul (Sender / Receiver): Führt I-PDU-Assembly, Truncation, Parsen und PDU-Verifikation aus; triggert kryptografische Primitive via CSM-APIs ( Csm_MacGenerate , Csm_MacVerify ). Crypto Stack (CSM/CryIf/Crypto Driver): Verwaltet den symmetrischen Schlüssel $K$ ( Secret Key , z. B. AES-128 für CMAC) im HSM, vHsm oder Secure Memory. D

Das Diagramm spannt den Bogen von der Anwendungsschicht über die Basissoftware (Service Layer, ECU Abstraction Layer, MCAL, Complex Drivers) bis hin zur zugrundeliegenden Mikrocontroller-Hardware (Hardware Security Module). 2. Funktionale Einordnung: AUTOSAR Classic Platform (ab Release R23-11), BSW Communication Services Layer, Modul SecOC (Secure Onboard Communication). * **Technischer Zweck:** Das Diagramm veranschaulicht die vertikale Durchgängigkeit des AUTOSAR Classic Crypto-Stacks (von der Applikation bis zur Hardware) sowie das Zusammenspiel von **Kanälen (Channels)**, **Krypto-Treibern (Crypto Drivers)** und den **zweistufigen Warteschlangen-Mechanismen (CSM Queuing vs. Crypto Driver Queuing)** bei der asynchronen/parallelen Abarbeitung von Krypto-Jobs (hier via HSM).
### 2. Beteiligte Komponenten & Entitäten
#### Schichten (Layers):
* **Application Layer:** Beherbergt die Software-Komponenten (SW-Cs) `App1`, `App2` und `App3`.
* **Runtime Environment (RTE):** Vermittlungsschicht für Service-Aufrufe zwischen Applikation und Basis-Software.
* **Service Layer:** Beinhaltet den standardisierten **CSM (Crypto Service Manager)**.
* **ECU Abstraction Layer:** Beinhaltet das **Crypto Interface (`CryIf`)**.
* **Microcontroller Abstraction Layer (MCAL):** Beinhaltet den hardwarenahen **Crypto Driver (`Crypto`)**.
* **Complex Drivers (CDD):** Vertikale Komponente rechts, die Schichten übergreift (hier als Referenz zur Standard-AUTOSAR-Architektur dargestellt).
* **Microcontroller (HW):** Hardware-Ebene mit integriertem **HSM (Hardware Security Module)**.
#### Software- & Hardware-Entitäten:
* **Applikationen:**
* `App1`: Fordert AES-Verschlüsselung/-Entschlüsselung an.
* `App2`: Fordert ebenfalls AES-Operationen an.
* `App3`: Fordert RSA-Krypto-Operationen (z. B. Signatur/Verifikation/Asymmetrisch) an.
* **Kanäle (Channels):**
* `Channel HW-AES`: Logischer Kanal für AES-Operationen, der vom CSM über CryIf zum Crypto Driver führt.
* `Channel HW-RSA`: Logischer Kanal für RSA-Operationen.
* **Hardware-Objekte (Crypto Driver Objects im HSM):**
* `HW-AES`: Dedizierter Hardware-Beschleuniger / Krypto-Core für symmetrische AES-Berechnungen.
* `HW-RSA`: Dedizierter Hardware-Beschleuniger für asymmetrische RSA-Berechnungen.
* **Jobs in Bearbeitung / Queues:**
* `AES high`: Hochpriorer AES-Job, aktuell in Abarbeitung im `HW-AES`.
* `AES low`: Niedrigpriorer AES-Job, wartend in der Warteschlange des Treibers (`Crypto driver queuing`).
* `RSA`: RSA-Job, aktuell in Abarbeitung im `HW-RSA`.
### 3. Technische Abläufe & Beziehungen
1. **Job-Generierung & Routing:**
* `App1` und `App2` initiieren Krypto-Jobs (AES) über standardisierte RTE-/CSM-Services (z. B. `Csm_Encrypt`, `Csm_Decrypt` bzw. allgemeines Job-Interface `Csm_JobStart` / `Csm_JobProcess`).
* Beide AES-Jobs werden demselben logischen CSM-Kanal (`Channel HW-AES`) zugeordnet.
* `App3` setzt einen asymmetrischen Auftrag (RSA) über `Channel HW-RSA` ab.
2. **Weiterleitung über das Crypto Interface (`CryIf`):**
* Die Kanäle durchqueren das `CryIf`. Dieses dient als Dispatcher und mappt die logischen CSM-Channels auf die jeweiligen Treiber (`Crypto Driver`) bzw. Treiber-Objekte (`Crypto Driver Objects`).
3. **Warteschlangen- und Prioritätssteuerung (Queuing & Dispatching):**

* **Im Kanal HW-AES:** Der Treiber-Queue-Bereich (`Crypto driver queuing`) nimmt anstehende Anfragen auf. Da der HSM-Kern `HW-AES` mit dem Job `AES high` belegt ist, wird der nachfolgende Job `AES low` in der Treiber-Warteschlange gepuffert. Sobald `AES high` abgeschlossen ist, meldet die Hardware dies via Interrupt/Polling, und `AES low` wird als Nächstes zur Ausführung transferiert.
* **Im Kanal HW-RSA:** Der Job `RSA` wurde direkt an das freie Treiber-Objekt `HW-RSA` übergeben und wird dort parallel verarbeitet.
4. **Parallele Ausführung:**
* Da `HW-AES` und `HW-RSA` voneinander unabhängige Krypto-Hardware-Objekte im HSM darstellen, laufen die Jobs `AES high` und `RSA` vollständig zeitgleich/nebenläufig.
### 4. Besondere technische Details & Normative Hinweise
* **Zweistufiges Queuing (CSM Queuing vs. Driver Queuing):**
* Das Schaubild visualisiert zwei gestrichelte rote Ebenen: `CSM queuing` (oben im CSM) und `Crypto driver queuing` (unten im Crypto Driver).

* AUTOSAR erlaubt Queuing sowohl im CSM (`CsmJobQueueSize > 0`) als auch im Crypto Driver (`CryptoDriverObjectQueueSize > 0`). Ist die Warteschlange des Treibers voll oder deaktiviert, puffert der CSM. Ist Treiber-Queuing aktiv, werden Jobs bevorzugt in den Crypto Driver geschleust, um Latenzen bei Hardware-Übernahmen zu minimieren.
* **Kanalbündelung (N:1-Beziehung Applikation zu Channel):**

* Mehrere Applikationen (`App1`, `App2`) können denselben Kanal nutzen. Ein Kanal bindet typischerweise an genau ein primitives Treiber-Objekt oder einen Pool (`CryIfChannel` $\rightarrow$ `CryptoDriverObject`).
* **Priorisierung (`jobPriority`):**
* Die Unterscheidung `AES high` vs. `AES low` verweist auf das Attribut `CsmJobPriority`. Bei aktiviertem Queuing werden Jobs innerhalb der Warteschlange nach Priorität sortiert abgearbeitet.
* **Synchroner vs. asynchroner Modus (`processingMode`):**

* Die gezeigte Entkopplung mit Queuing und separater Hardware-Abarbeitung im HSM verdeutlicht den asynchronen Verarbeitungsmodus (`CRYPTO_PROCESSING_ASYNC`), bei dem die Fertigstellung über Callback-Benachrichtigungen (`Csm_CallbackNotification`) signalisiert wird.
### 5. Zusammenfassung für Entwickler

Das Schaubild verdeutlicht, wie Krypto-Jobs aus mehreren Applikationen über konfigurierbare Kanäle parallelisiert und hardwarenah priorisiert werden. Für Entwickler und Integratoren ist entscheidend, Kanäle und Puffergrößen (`CsmQueueSize` und `CryptoDriverObjectQueueSize`) sorgfältig auf die verfügbaren Hardware-Objekte des HSM abzustimmen, um Blockaden bei zeitkritischen Krypto-Operationen (wie `AES high`) durch niederpriore Tasks zu verhindern.

7.2.1.3 Asynchronous Job Processing
[SWS_Csm_00036]
Upstream requirements: SRS_CryptoStack_00101
⌈If the asynchronous interface is used, the interface functions shall only hand over the
necessary information to the underlying Crypto Stack modules.⌋
[SWS_Csm_00039]
Upstream requirements: SRS_CryptoStack_00082
⌈The users of the CSM shall be notified when a requested cryptographic service has
been processed by calling the callback function from the job primitive configuration.⌋

7.2.1 Normal Operation
[SWS_Csm_01039]
Upstream requirements: SRS_CryptoStack_00084
⌈To unite a single call function and the streaming approach for the crypto services,
there is the mode parameter, which determines the operation mode. This service op-
eration is a flag field, indicating the operation mode "START", "UPDATE" or "FINISH".
It declares explicitly what operation shall be performed. These operation modes can
be mixed, and execute multiple operations at once.
The diagram in [SWS_Crypto_00018] (in [4]) shows the state machine of a job of this
design.⌋
Note: The actual transaction of the states is made in the layer, which works with these
states, i.e. in the Crypto Driver.
[SWS_Csm_01033] ⌈The CSM crypto services shall support to process multiple op-
eration mode inputs with a single call.⌋
[SWS_Csm_01045] ⌈If the CRYPTO_OPERATIONMODE_START and CRYPTO_OPER-
ATIONMODE_FINISH bits are set and the CRYPTO_OPERATIONMODE_UPDATE is not
set, the Csm_<Service> function shall return with E_NOT_OK.⌋
Note: The coherent single call approach could improve the performance due to less
overhead. Instead of calling the explicit API multiple times, only one call is neces-
sary. This approach is intended to be used with small data input, which demand fast
processing.
While operating with the streaming approach ("Start", "Update", "Finish") the dedicated
Crypto Driver Object is waiting for further input ("Update") until the "Finish" state has
been reached. No other job could be processed on this Crypto Driver instance mean-
while.

7.2.2.2.2 Queuing
The CSM may have several queues, where the jobs are lining up depending on their
priority, to process multiple cryptographic requests. The path from a CSM queue via
the CryIf to a Crypto Driver Object is called a channel. Each queue of the CSM is
mapped to one channel to access the crypto primitives of the Crypto Driver Object.
The size of the queue is configurable.
To optimize the hardware usage of the Crypto Driver Object, there is optionally a queue
in Crypto Driver, too.
A Crypto Driver Object represents an instance of an independent crypto "device" (hard-
ware or software, e.g. AES accelerator). There could be a channel for fast AES and
CMAC calculations on an HSM for jobs with high priority, which ends on a native AES
calculation service in the Crypto Driver. But it is also possible, that a Crypto Driver Ob-
ject is a piece of software, e.g. for RSA calculations where users are able to encrypt,
decrypt, sign or verify data.
Figure 7.4: AUTOSAR Layered View with channels
Figure 7.4 illustrates an AUTOSAR Layered View with channels. In this example, there
is a HSM with two Crypto Driver Objects (HW-AES and HW-RSA), each of them has an
own channel. Each channel is connected to a CSM queue and a Crypto Driver Object
queue.
In this case, both Crypto Driver Objects are processing a crypto job (AES-high and
RSA) each, while the queue of the Crypto Driver Object contains one more job (AES-
low). If the HW-AES of the HSM finished the AES-high job, AES-low job will be pro-
cessed as next one.
Other scenarios with the same setup (without jobs in process or in queues) can be
derived as follows: It will be assumed, that a new job of an application calls RSA.
• If the Crypto Driver Object of the RSA is not busy, the job will be processed
immediately.
• If the Crypto Driver Object of the RSA is busy, but the queue of the Crypto Driver
Object is not full, the job will be listed into that queue in order of its priority. As
soon as the Crypto Driver Object is free, the job with the highest priority from the
Crypto Driver Object queue will be executed.
• If the Crypto Driver Object of the RSA is busy and the queue of the Crypto Driver
Object is full, the job will be stored in the CSM queue in order of its priority.
• If the Crypto Driver Object of the RSA is busy and the queue of the Crypto Driver
Object as well as the CSM queue are full, the CSM rejects the request.
• If the Crypto Driver Object of the RSA is active, the job is already started in
the Crypto Driver and is waiting for either more data to process or the finish
command.

Synchronous job processing and queuing might not be useful. So, if synchronous job
processing is chosen, the queue sizes should be "0". However, it is also possible to
use channels (including queues) with synchronous and asynchronous jobs.
The queued jobs can be passed to the CRYIF in the Csm_MainFunction.
If the job has the state "active" the CSM shall assume, that the mapped cryptographic
driver instance is currently processing this job and the caller wants to continue with the
operation (e.g. feeding more data using "update"). The plausibility check has to be
performed in the cryptographic driver instance.

8.3.2 Job Processing Interface
To unite a single call function and a streaming approach for the crypto services, there
is one interface CryIf_ProcessJob. Its job parameter job contains a Crypto_-
OperationModeType flag field (job->jobPrimitiveInputOutput.mode), which can be
set as "START", "UPDATE", "FINISH" or combination of them. It declares explicitly
what operation shall be performed. These operation modes can be mixed, and execute
multiple operations at once.
To process a crypto service with a single call with Crypto_ProcessJob the operation
mode is a disjunction of the 3 modes "START|UPDATE|FINISH".

8.3.8.5 Key Generation Interface
The key generation interface is used to generate a key into the key element CRYPTO_-
KE_KEYGENERATE_KEY according to the algorithm defined in the key element
CRYPTO_KE_KEYGENERATE_ALGORITHM.
The key will be generated from the random value that is located in the key element
CRYPTO_KE_KEYGENERATE_SEED.
The random value can be generated, for example, with the function Csm_Random-
Generate and must be stored in CRYPTO_KE_KEYGENERATE_SEED before the key
generation is triggered.
It is important to check the quality of the randomness and its entropy of the seed, which
depends on the used hardware, and software of a stack. The randomness has a major
impact on the quality of the generated key material.
The key element with the id=CRYPTO_KE_KEYGENERATE_ALGORITHM contains a type
from Crypto_AlgorithmFamilyType, e.g. CRYPTO_ALGOFAM_AES, CRYPTO_AL-
GOFAM_RSA or CRYPTO_ALGOFAM_ED25519, that allows to generate an adequate key.
As a counter example, the algorithm family type CRYPTO_ALGOFAM_SHA2_256 is not
adequate because it provides no hint what key shall be generated.
For the key element CRYPTO_KE_KEYGENERATE_KEY the key element configuration
item CryptoKeyElement/CryptoKeyElementFormat indicates the format of the
generated key.

8.3.8.7 Key Exchange Interface
Two users that each have a private secret can use a key exchange protocol to obtain
a common secret, e.g. a key for a symmetric-key algorithm, without telling each other
their private secret and without any listener being able to obtain the common secret or
their private secrets.
The functions Csm_KeyExchangeCalcPubVal / Csm_JobKeyExchangeCalcPub-
Val and Csm_KeyExchangeCalcSecret / Csm_JobKeyExchangeCalcSecret
are used to support Diffie-Hellman (DH) key exchange.
This allows two partners, Alice and Bob, to generate private and public key material, to
exchange public parts so that both parties can generate at the end a common shared
secret. This shared secret can further be used, e.g. for symmetric data operation such
as data encryption or MAC generation.
The public and private key material can either be based on prime based large number
as it is used with RSA or on elliptic curve (so-called elliptic-curve diffie-hellman).
The CSM key exchange functions require a key with key elements according
to [SWS_Csm_01022], in the line of Crypto Service "Key Exchange".
The key
elements CRYPTO_KE_KEYEXCHANGE_BASE, CRYPTO_KE_KEYEXCHANGE_PRIVKEY
and CRYPTO_KE_KEYEXCHANGE_OWNPUBKEY are used to hold the public/private key
material.

Figure 7.1: AUTOSAR Layered View with Crypto Driver Module The Crypto Driver module is located in the micro controller abstraction layer and is be- low the Crypto Interface module and Crypto Service Manager module. It implements a generic interface for synchronous and asynchronous cryptographic primitives. It also supports key storage, key configuration, and key management for cryptographic ser- vices. T o provide cryptographic functionalities an ECU needs to integrate one unique Crypto Service Manager module and one Crypto Interface. However, the Crypto Interface can access several Crypto Drivers, each of them is configured according to the underlying Crypto Driver Object. A Crypto Driver Object represents an instance of independent crypto hardware "device" (e.g. AES accelerator). There could be a channel for fast AES and CMAC calculations on an HSM for jobs with high priority , which ends on a native AES calculation service in the Crypto Driver. But it is also possible, that a Crypto Driver Object is a piece of software, e.g. for RSA calculations where jobs are able to encrypt, decrypt, sign or verify data. The Crypto Driver Object is the endpoint of a crypto channel.

Figure 7.4: Integration into AUTOSAR Their differential treatment is due to the underlying trust-model: system services (Functional Clusters ) are the trusted foundation while Adaptive Applica- tions are untrusted additions. T o ensure secure access from application side the trust-model, in the form of IAM, is designed for and applied only to Adaptive Ap- plications. Similarly , the exclusive-access-model aims at protecting an applica- tion’s own resources against access by other applications, but additionally also against access by Functional Clusters other than FC Crypto . On the other hand some Functional Clusters specify their own key-slots, which contain key-material to be used when implementing certain system services (e.g. secure data storage, secure di- agnostics or secure communication such as SecOC). Because key-management of Key Slots used by Functional Clusters should be possible from an Adap- tive Application (e.g. OEM key manager), the exclusive-access-model defines two types of Key Slots : • application: the application has exclusive access to this key slot. It is able to import/export, update/delete and use the contained key-material. No other appli- cation or Functional Cluster may access this Key Slot . • machine: this type of Key Slot is defined by the adaptive machine and may be used by the Functional Cluster for which it is configured. Additionally , the Key Slot may be assigned to a single Adaptive Application that is then able to manage the contained key-material.

7.2.1 Normal Operation
[SWS_Crypto_00017] ⌈"START" indicates a new request of a crypto primitive, and it
shall cancel all previous requests of the same job.⌋
Note:
"job is being processed" means that the corresponding crypto driver object is currently
and actively processing this job. When a job is not finished but the crypto driver object
is not active with it (because, e.g., the operation "FINISH" is outstanding) this does not
mean that this job is being processed.
Note:
To unite a single call function and a streaming approach for the crypto services, there
is one interface Crypto_ProcessJob with a service operation parameter (embedded
in job structure parameter). This service operation is a flag field, that indicates the op-
eration modes "START", "UPDATE" or "FINISH". It declares explicitly which operation
will be performed.
If the "UPDATE" flag is set, the crypto primitive expects input data. "FINISH" indicates,
that after this function call, all data are fed completely and the crypto primitive can
finalize the calculations.
These operations can be combined to execute multiple operations at once. Then, the
operations are performed in the order "START", "UPDATE", "FINISH".
The coherent single call approach could improve the performance due to less over-
head. Instead of calling the explicit API multiple times, only one call is necessary. This
approach is intended to be used with small data input, which demand fast processing.

7.2.3 Design Notes
The Crypto Driver provides two services: (1) the crypto services itself and (2) key
management.

7.2.4 Key Management
A key consists of one or more key elements.
Examples of key elements are the key material itself, an initialization vector, a seed
state for random number generation, or the proof of the SHE standard.
Each key element has a defined access right for read or write access. The access right
itself is defined by enumerations with an assigned value (see [ECUC_Crypto_00024] or
[ECUC_Crypto_00027]) in the configuration of a CryptoKeyElement. The integer val-
ues of these enumerations are chosen in a way, that the assignment of an access right
to a key element also deduces further right accesses. The lower the value, the higher
the access right. This allows an easy compare of the assigned value to a required right
access by numbers.
Example:
If
a
key
element
has
access
rights
of
CRYPTO_RA_INTERNAL_COPY=2,
the
right
permission
also
applies
to
CRYPTO_RA_ENCRYPTED=1
and
CRYPTO_RA_ALLOWED=0,
because both rights of the assigned enumeration
values are lower and therefore are lower in the ranking of the access rights.
[SWS_Crypto_00219] ⌈Access rights shall be taken into account when direct access
to key elements are required. This applies for read and write access.⌋

for example, to store keys in one driver channel that provides secure key storage and to
distribute them to other driver implementations that have no such capabilities. However,

7.2.5.3 Definition of SHE key material
[SWS_Crypto_00255] ⌈If a crypto key element is used as a secret key of a SHE hard-
ware, then the configuration of CryptoKeyFormat/CryptoKeyElementFormat shall be
set to CRYPTO_KE_FORMAT_BIN_SHEKEY. This indicates that the key element shall
be presented in M1M2M3 format as specified in [6]. The function Crypto_KeyEle-
mentSet is used to load the key into the SHE hardware (not directly on a call to this
function but rather through key-set-valid operation).
With Crypto_KeyElementSet, the parameter ’keyElementId’ shall be set to 1. This
can be taken from e.g. CRYPTO_KE_MAC_KEY or CRYPTO_KE_CIPHER_KEY (see
[SWS_Csm_01022]).
The SHE hardware provides M4M5 as the proof of the correct key processing and to
confirm the operation. To extract this key information, an additional key element is
needed. To read the proof after the key-set-valid operation, the function Crypto_-
KeyElementGet with key element ID value ’2’ shall be used, e.g. with pre-defined
macros CRYPTO_KE_MAC_PROOF or CRYPTO_KE_CIPHER_PROOF. The proof
will only be available directly after a successful key-element-set followed by key-set-
valid operation, e.g. within an ignition cycle. This means, the proof must not be stored,
e.g. in NV-RAM, to provide this information later on.⌋

7.2.5 Key Formats
The key element with ID 1 is a particular key that provides the cryptographic key for the
related cryptographic primitive.
In IETF RFC, keys are described in a specific format to provide a common and compact
way to transport them between entities.
To support this standard also within AUTOSAR, the following chapter describes key
formats that are supported by AUTOSAR.
This allows to provide a given key in such a format to the crypto driver, e.g. from parts
of a certificate without the needs for an application to analyse the structure and to
construct that data.
By supporting the IETF RFC within the crypto driver, the key material can be provided
as is.
If supported, the extraction of the required key elements, such as private or public key
fields, is accomplished in the driver.
It is unlikely to compose such formats back to the application by the crypto driver.
Thus, such a key element might only be temporarily stored and may not persisted in
"composed" format (M1M2M3), e.g. to retrieve that after reset.

7.2.6.1 Writing keys to NVM
[SWS_Crypto_00242]
Upstream requirements: SRS_CryptoStack_00061
⌈The storage of keys resp. their elements shall be initiated only when KEYSETVALID"
is started, either by a call to Crypto_KeySetValid or to Crypto_ProcessJob with
primitive service CRYPTO_KEYSETVALID or CRYPTO_KEYSETINVALID set. Thus,
key element storage in NVM shall not be initiated on a call to Crypto_KeyEle-
mentSet or similar operation. The storage operation shall only take place if the vali-
dation was successfully finished and the operation returns E_OK (either directly by a
synchronous call or asynchronously through the callback).⌋
Rationale:
Especially when key elements of a key have interdependencies to one or more other
key element(s) of the same key, writing the key element immediately when it is set
has the risk, that the key itself can be inconsistent. In addition, the explicit initiation
of the operation with KEYSETVALID allows the crypto driver to check the consistency
and interdependency of all elements and storing will be denied if the check fails. Also,
updating several elements of a key will result in a single write operation to NVM and
not multiple times for each key element, which can reduce the total number of write
operations to NVM.

7.2.6 Key Storage in NVM
To allow a crypto driver to persist key elements in non-volatile memory, access to NVM
is required. For this, the configuration of the crypto driver needs a reference to one or
more NVM blocks. Keys with key elements that shall be persisted are to be assigned
to these blocks. The elements that are to be persisted will then be written by the driver
on validation and values are retrieved during initialization of the driver. The principal
relation to configuration items is shown in Figure 7-2.
Figure 7.2: NvBlock configuration for key persistence
Important note:
The crypto driver only deals with the functional operation to store data to and read data
from an NVM block. Any error handling like defects of NVM blocks must be captured
and dealt with in the application.

7.2.7.2 Custom service and function profile 1 (KeyM and certificate manage-
ment)
This profile defines how to use a custom service with the certificate management ser-
vices specified for the KeyM. Using this profile enables the KeyM to forward the actual
certificate processing to the Crypto Driver and its associated HSM. The Crypto profile
provides a consistent mapping of the parameters from the KeyM services and functions
to the Csm job configured for the custom service and to the custom synchronous API
function Crypto_CustomSync.
The ServiceInfoType is defined as CUSTOM_SERVICE with value 0x15.
The Crypto_AlgorithmFamilyType is defined as CRYPTO_ALGOFAM_KEYM with
value 0x80 and need to be configured via [ECUC_Crypto_00047] CryptoPrimitiveAl-
gorithmFamilyCustomId.
The Crypto_AlgorithmModeType is defined as CRYPTO_ALGOMODE_NOT_SET with
value 0x00.
The KeyM_ServiceCertificate (ServiceId: 0x09) can be mapped by the KeyM to call
KeyM_ServiceCertificateByCertId (ServiceId: 0x13).
In case the data type mapped to a parameter of type unit8* have a bigger size (e.g.
uint16) the MSB should be the first byte.

2.4.10 Modeling of services
Services are provided through ports.
A port implements a port interface.
A
port interface can be a ClientServerInterface, a SenderReceiverInterface or a
ModeSwitchInterface.

defines return, input and output parameters. Each service operation has a relation-
ship to an existing api function (c function). Blueprints allow to configure things like
parameters, services, ...
A SenderReceiverInterface defines DataElements.
Each data element have to be
linked to a data type.
A ModeSwitchInterface defines modes within a ModeDeclarationGroup.

Example #1:
A ciphersuite that references RSA provides TcpIpTlsCsmKeyExchangeEncryp-

Example #2:
A ciphersuite references ECDHE_ECDSA and the used certificate contains appropri-
ate ECC keys, ECDSA capable in this case.
The server generates DH-parameter
using the crypto job Csm_KeyExchangeCalcPubVal() using the reference to
TcpIpTlsCsmKeyExchangeKeyRef and signs the result using TcpIpTlsHand-

must be copied accordingly (see Example #1). The resulting data is sent to the TLS
client, who verifies the certificate and uses the key of the certificate to verify the pro-

5.1.3 Streaming Approach vs Single Call Approach.
The processing of a crypto service embraces the operations "START", "UPDATE", and
"FINISH":
• "START" (CRYPTO_OPERATIONMODE_START) notifies about a new start of a
particular job and initializes the cryptographic computations;
• Input
data
can
be
provided
using
the
"UPDATE"
mode
(CRYPTO_OPERATIONMODE_UPDATE) and intermediate results are com-
puted;
• "FINISH" (CRYPTO_OPERATIONMODE_FINISH) indicates that the final crypto-
graphic calculations shall be performed.
[SWS_Crypto_00018] gives an overview of the job’s state machine, based on the afore-
said operations. The requested operation is given as operation mode parameter to a
CSM job.
Crypto services can be invoked using a streaming or a single call approach.
The
streaming approach performs single operations separately on a given data.
The
streaming approach is available by calling, e.g., Csm_MacGenerate separately for
each operation mode. Using the streaming approach allows, for example, the pro-
cessing of very huge input data by calling the service function with operation mode
"UPDATE" several times.
In order to increase performance of the crypto services, the single call approach com-
bines several job operations into one single function invocation. This reduces the over-
head of calling the function several times. The operation modes declare which op-
eration shall be performed and can be combined. The operations are performed in
the order "START", "UPDATE", "FINISH". In

7.1 Crypto key submodule
The crypto key submodule is used to initialize, update and maintain cryptographic key
material for an ECU. One use case is the provision of keys for the secured on-board
communication that need to be distributed to the involved ECUs. These keys should
be provided to CSM keys which are assigned to crypto jobs that are used for authen-
tication of Secured I-PDUs. It is therefore crucial from a modelling aspect to assign
the keys provided by the key master to the CSM keys and jobs used for the respective
Secured-I PDUs. This is an overall task in a vehicle and affects several ECUs in the
same way. It is one purpose of the crypto key submodule to support this operation.
The key master can either be located directly in the vehicle to coordinate the key gen-
eration internally, e.g. as a particular ECU. It is also possible to use a backend system
in the cloud that generates the key material and provides the necessary data in a se-
cure way to the ECUs. Usually diagnostic commands are used for the communication,
directly or indirectly, between the key master and the crypto key sub module.

7.2.2.2.2 Queuing
The CSM may have several queues, where the jobs are lining up depending on their
priority, to process multiple cryptographic requests. The path from a CSM queue via
the CryIf to a Crypto Driver Object is called a channel. Each queue of the CSM is
mapped to one channel to access the crypto primitives of the Crypto Driver Object.
The size of the queue is configurable.
To optimize the hardware usage of the Crypto Driver Object, there is optionally a queue
in Crypto Driver, too.
A Crypto Driver Object represents an instance of an independent crypto "device" (hard-
ware or software, e.g. AES accelerator). There could be a channel for fast AES and
CMAC calculations on an HSM for jobs with high priority, which ends on a native AES
calculation service in the Crypto Driver. But it is also possible, that a Crypto Driver Ob-
ject is a piece of software, e.g. for RSA calculations where users are able to encrypt,
decrypt, sign or verify data.

7.2.2.5 Job context interface
The job context interface allows to save or restore the context data of the workspace
for a specific crypto service from the crypto driver. This allows to store all dynamically
created data within a crypto driver so that it can later be restored to continue this
operation at the exact point where the context snapshot was taken.
Key element data are not affected. This means, that key elements are not part of
the context data and must be set or read by the key element interface separately if
necessary.

7.2.7.2 Custom service and function profile 1 (KeyM and certificate manage-
ment)
This profile defines how to use a custom service with the certificate management ser-
vices specified for the KeyM. Using this profile enables the KeyM to forward the actual
certificate processing to the Crypto Driver and its associated HSM. The Crypto profile
provides a consistent mapping of the parameters from the KeyM services and functions
to the Csm job configured for the custom service and to the custom synchronous API
function Crypto_CustomSync.
The ServiceInfoType is defined as CUSTOM_SERVICE with value 0x15.
The Crypto_AlgorithmFamilyType is defined as CRYPTO_ALGOFAM_KEYM with
value 0x80 and need to be configured via [ECUC_Crypto_00047] CryptoPrimitiveAl-
gorithmFamilyCustomId.
The Crypto_AlgorithmModeType is defined as CRYPTO_ALGOMODE_NOT_SET with
value 0x00.
The KeyM_ServiceCertificate (ServiceId: 0x09) can be mapped by the KeyM to call
KeyM_ServiceCertificateByCertId (ServiceId: 0x13).
In case the data type mapped to a parameter of type unit8* have a bigger size (e.g.
uint16) the MSB should be the first byte.

7.4.2.10.2 Verify Certificates
[SWS_Dcm_01459] Supported communicationConfiguration
Upstream requirements: RS_Diag_04230
⌈On reception of an Authentication (0x29) service with sub-function equal to verifyC-
ertificateUnidirectional or verifyCertificateBidirectional, the Dcm shall reply with an NRC
0x31 (requestOutOfRange) if the communicationConfiguration (COCO) parameter has
a value different than 0x00.⌋
The support of a COCO with constant value of 0x00 implies that no session key is
supported by the Dcm. Upon receiving an authentication request with sub-function ver-
ifyCertificateUniDirectional and the communicationConfiguration (COCO) set to 0x00,
the Dcm starts to verify the certificate. This service is implemented on BSW level by in-
tention, to reduce the possible dialects of service 0x29 to what is natively supported by
AUTOSAR. The Csm [17] and KeyM [18] modules allow to use different cryptographic
methods. It is part of the Dcm strategy to explicitly require that certificates and all kind
of access to information inside are handled by the Csm and its configuration. This
allows to map different kind of certificates with different levels of security to the Dcm,
thus abstracting the certificate complexity from Dcm.

7.4 ChrgM Charging Control Messages
The ChrgM has two sets of messages to control AC and DC charging. It also offers two
different sets of messages depending on whether EiM or PnC is selected as a payment
method.

7.4 ISO15118Chrg Charging Control Messages

offers two different sets of messages depending on whether EiM or PnC is selected as
a payment method.

7.8.2.1 Authenticity of QSEvs
IdsM can optionally protect the authenticity of QSEvs using cryptographic au-
thenticator generated by the Csm in conjunction with the crypto stack. It can be
used to ensure authenticity as well as to prove integrity of messages from the
IdsM via all communication systems until reaching the Backend or SOC (End2End-
Security).
[SWS_IdsM_01204] Authenticating QSEv
Upstream requirements: RS_Ids_00505, RS_Ids_00630
⌈The IdsM shall be able to attach a cryptographic authenticator, with the same
data format, to each QSEv. The authentication feature is optional and shall be
activated or deactivated globally for all QSEvs by setting the parameter IdsMAuthen-
ticatorSupport to TRUE or FALSE.⌋
[SWS_IdsM_01205] AuthenticatorLength
Upstream requirements: RS_Ids_00505, RS_Ids_00630
⌈The IdsM’s parameter IdsMAuthenticatorLength shall define the length in bytes
of the authenticator calculated by the crypto services. It shall be configured when
the authentication feature is activated.⌋
The IdsM’s Csm Job IdsMCsmJobReference has two different types of authenti-
cation processing: synchronous and asynchronous. This processing is configured in
the Csm Job Primitive linked to the Csm Job, and determines the internal handling of
the IdsM for the authentication.
[SWS_IdsM_01206] GenerateAuthenticator
Upstream requirements: RS_Ids_00505, RS_Ids_00630
⌈In order to generate an authenticator by a Csm job IdsMCsmJobReference,
the authentication generation shall be triggered by calling the Csm function Csm_
SignatureGenerate or Csm_MacGenerate depending on the selected IdsMAu-
thenticatorType.⌋
Manager
[SWS_IdsM_01207] SynchronousAuthenticatorGeneration
Upstream requirements: RS_Ids_00505, RS_Ids_00630
⌈If the authenticator is generated by a synchronous Csm job IdsMCsmJobRefer-
ence, when the function Csm_SignatureGenerate or Csm_MacGenerate returns,
the authenticator shall be immediately available.⌋
[SWS_IdsM_01208] AsynchronousAuthenticatorGeneration
Upstream requirements: RS_Ids_00505, RS_Ids_00630
⌈If the authenticator is generated by an asynchronous Csm job IdsMCsmJobRef-
erence, the IdsM shall be informed about the generation of the authenticator by
Csm via the Csm notification callback function IdsM_CsmNotification.⌋
Note that the callback function IdsM_CsmNotification shall be configured in the
Csm Module as a Csm job primitive callback for the Csm Job configured for the IdsM.
Since the authenticator is used for all QSEvs, i.e. independent of their sink config-
urations, the authenticator shall be generated before the QSEv is distributed to its
configured sinks.
Over which data the authenticator shall be computed and how the authentica-
tor shall be included in the IDS Message Structure, is specified in [4, Specification of
Intrusion Detection System Protocol].

communication systems until reaching the Backend or SOC (End2End-Security).

The sensors coming from a SW-C or application have the option to report additional
information to the IdsM. The necessary configurations can be made per SEv via the
parameters in container IdsMServiceInterfaceOptions.

Upstream requirements: RS_Ids_00630

sion of the context data.IdsMEventMaxContextDataSize.⌋

forwarding context data of the corresponding security event, helps to avoid the waste
of resources caused by the copying of data done by the RTE. With this limit, the size

being sent.

8.3.2 Hash Interface
A cryptographic hash function is a deterministic procedure that takes an arbitrary block
of data and returns a fixed-size bit string, the hash value, such that an accidental or
intentional change to the data will change the hash value. Main properties of hash
functions are that it is infeasible to find a message that has a given hash or to find two
different messages with the same hash.

8.3.3 MAC Interface
A message authentication code (MAC) is a short piece of information used to authenti-
cate a message. A MAC algorithm accepts as input a secret key and an arbitrary-length
message to be authenticated, and outputs a MAC. The MAC value protects both a mes-
sage’s data integrity as well as its authenticity, by allowing verifiers (who also possess
the secret key) to detect any changes to the message content.

prove integrity of signed messages. If a message is digitally signed, any change in the
message after signature will invalidate the signature. Furthermore, there is no efficient
way to modify a message and its signature to produce a new message with a valid
signature.

The random interface provides generation of random numbers.
A random number
can be generated either by a physical device (true random number generator), or by
computational algorithms (pseudo random number generator). The randomness of
pseudo random number generators can be increased by an appropriate selection of
the seed.

this specification. If applicable, proper seeding actions shall be done prior to request
any random numbers.

generators. Especially if no true random number generator (TRNG) in hardware is
available for generation of random numbers.

this specification. If applicable, proper seeding actions shall be done prior to request
any random numbers.

generators. Especially if no true random number generator (TRNG) in hardware is
available for generation of random numbers.

8.3.8.5 Key Generation Interface
The key generation interface is used to generate a key into the key element CRYPTO_-
KE_KEYGENERATE_KEY according to the algorithm defined in the key element
CRYPTO_KE_KEYGENERATE_ALGORITHM.
The key will be generated from the random value that is located in the key element
CRYPTO_KE_KEYGENERATE_SEED.
The random value can be generated, for example, with the function Csm_Random-
Generate and must be stored in CRYPTO_KE_KEYGENERATE_SEED before the key
generation is triggered.
It is important to check the quality of the randomness and its entropy of the seed, which
depends on the used hardware, and software of a stack. The randomness has a major
impact on the quality of the generated key material.
The key element with the id=CRYPTO_KE_KEYGENERATE_ALGORITHM contains a type
from Crypto_AlgorithmFamilyType, e.g. CRYPTO_ALGOFAM_AES, CRYPTO_AL-
GOFAM_RSA or CRYPTO_ALGOFAM_ED25519, that allows to generate an adequate key.
As a counter example, the algorithm family type CRYPTO_ALGOFAM_SHA2_256 is not
adequate because it provides no hint what key shall be generated.
For the key element CRYPTO_KE_KEYGENERATE_KEY the key element configuration
item CryptoKeyElement/CryptoKeyElementFormat indicates the format of the
generated key.

8.3.8.7 Key Exchange Interface
Two users that each have a private secret can use a key exchange protocol to obtain
a common secret, e.g. a key for a symmetric-key algorithm, without telling each other
their private secret and without any listener being able to obtain the common secret or
their private secrets.
The functions Csm_KeyExchangeCalcPubVal / Csm_JobKeyExchangeCalcPub-
Val and Csm_KeyExchangeCalcSecret / Csm_JobKeyExchangeCalcSecret
are used to support Diffie-Hellman (DH) key exchange.
This allows two partners, Alice and Bob, to generate private and public key material, to
exchange public parts so that both parties can generate at the end a common shared
secret. This shared secret can further be used, e.g. for symmetric data operation such
as data encryption or MAC generation.
The public and private key material can either be based on prime based large number
as it is used with RSA or on elliptic curve (so-called elliptic-curve diffie-hellman).
The CSM key exchange functions require a key with key elements according
to [SWS_Csm_01022], in the line of Crypto Service "Key Exchange".
The key
elements CRYPTO_KE_KEYEXCHANGE_BASE, CRYPTO_KE_KEYEXCHANGE_PRIVKEY
and CRYPTO_KE_KEYEXCHANGE_OWNPUBKEY are used to hold the public/private key
material.
These values can either be pre-defined and set by Csm_KeyElementSet followed by
Csm_KeySetValid or generated. For example, these key values can be generated by

8.3.8 Key Management Interface
The following interfaces are used for key management. Basically, a key contains of one
ore more key elements. A key element can be part of multiple keys. For example, this
allows to derive a key element from a password with one keyId, and to use this derived
key element for encryption with another keyId.
Note: If the actual key element to be modified is directly mapped to flash memory, there
could be a bigger delay when calling the key management functions (synchronous
operation)

2 Acronyms and Abbreviations

2 Acronyms and Abbreviations
The glossary below includes acronyms and abbreviations that are only relevant to
Intrusion Detection System Manager. A general list of acronyms and abbre-
viations is available in the [1, AUTOSAR glossary].
Acronym
Description:
Filter Chain
A set of consecutive filters which is applied to Security Events-
Intrusion Detection System
An Intrusion Detection System is a security control which detects
and processes security events.
Intrusion
Detection
System
Manager
The Intrusion Detection System Manager handles security events
reported by security sensors.
Intrusion Detection System Re-
porter
The Intrusion Detection System Reporter handles qualified secu-
rity events received from Idsm instances.
Security Extract
The Security Extract specifies which security events are handled
by IdsM instances and their configuration parameters.
Security Event Type
A security event type can be identified by its security event type
ID. Instances of security event types are called security events
and share the same security event type ID.
Security Events
Onboard Security Events are instances of security event types
which are reported by BSW or SWC to the IdsM.
Security Event Memory
A user defined diagnostic event memory which is independent
from the primary diagnostic event memory.
Security Sensors
BSW or SWC which report security events to the Idsm.
Qualified Security Events
Security events which pass their filter chain are regarded as
Qualified Security Events.

7.3.2 Security Event Definition
A Security Event or Security Event Instance SEv defines the atomic unit, reported by a
sensor, that can be handled by the IdsM module. The IdsM receives the notification
of a sensor from BSW or CDD modules, or from SW-Cs via the RTE. The IdsM mod-
ule uses the EventId to manage the status of the SEv of a system and performs the
required actions for individual results, e.g., filtering, storing, reporting via the network.
A Security Event Definition represents the type of event to be reported. The defini-
tion, found in the SecXT, includes a global unique identifier and the short-name of the
reporting module.

7.4 Meta Data Handling
Meta data of PDUs is supported by a large number of modules of the communication
stack. It serves to transport information through the layers, that is in general abstracted
by the layered architecture. The first supported meta data was the CAN ID of PDUs
related to CanIf.
The meta data is transported by the PduInfoType structure via a separate pointer
to a byte array alongside the length of and a pointer to the payload of the PDU. The
content of the meta data is defined by the EcuC description of the global PDU (/-
EcuC/EcucConfigSet/EcucPduCollection/Pdu), which gives types (MetaData
ItemType), lengths (MetaDataItemLength) and the ordering of meta data items (
MetaDataItem) contained in the meta data of a certain PDU.

segment of a communication network, being a consumer for this Time Base.

7.5 Qualification of SEvs
Raw Security Events can be generated at a very high rate by the BSW. However,
only a subset of these events might be of interest to the OEM. By preprocessing the raw
SEv and dropping all events that do not match the filtering criteria, resource needs on
the ECUs and the network can be reduced.

7.6.2 Sampling Filters
The sampling filters forward only certain events out of all incoming security events.
These are filters specific to an instance of a SEv.

7.6.3 Aggregation Filters
All SEv of a given type occurring within a configured time interval are aggregated into
one SEv with an additional counter information attached that indicates how often the
event occurred in the time interval.

7.8.3 Storage of Events: Dem / Sem Sink
In order to use Dem as a sink to IdsM, the user must provide sufficient configuration,
namely, IdsMDemEventReference and IdsMSinkDem. The Dem event referenced
over IdsMDemEventReference is configured to have a callback to IdsM_DemRead-
QSEv and sufficient freeze frame size to accept the QSEv as specified in the IDS mes-
sage. Upon qualification of a security event, IdsM notifies a FAILED event to
Dem by calling the Dem_SetEventStatus and Dem subsequently calls IdsM over
IdsM_DemReadQSEv to fetch the IDS message. To conclude the storage of the
event in Dem, IdsM calls Dem_SetEventStatus again and reports the same event
as PASSED. The FAILED report to Dem, the callback to IdsM and the PASSED report
to Dem indicate the storage of a singular qualified security event. At most one
concurrent storage of qualified security event in Dem is supported.

7.8 Reporting and Persistence of SEVs
Once the filter chain has processed the incoming SEvs, the resulting events from the
processing filter chain are considered QSEvs.
Only QSEvs are further handled by the on-board IDS. These QSEvs can be either per-
sisted in memory, sent to another ECU, or both depending on the configuration. The
destination of a QSEv is called data sink.

Provides the destination buffer (SduDataPtr) and the number of

BUFREQ_E_BUSY is returned. The lower layer module may

copied data must remain in the TP buffer to be available for error
recovery. TP_DATACONF indicates that all data that has been
copied before this call is confirmed and can be removed from the
TP buffer. Data copied by this API call is excluded and will be
confirmed later. TP_DATARETRY indicates that this API call shall
copy previously copied data in order to recover from an error. In
this case TxTpDataCnt specifies the offset in bytes from the
current data copy position.

None

to determine the size of the following CFs.

BufReq_ReturnType
BUFREQ_OK: Data has been copied to the transmit buffer

BUFREQ_E_BUSY: Request could not be fulfilled, because the

BufReq_ReturnType IdsM_CopyTxData (

)
Service ID [hex]
0x43
Sync/Async
Synchronous
